# Week 3: Systematic Search

Systematic search retains an explicit account of alternatives.
It may explore some choices first because they look promising,
but it does not treat a disappointing guess as proof that the
remaining choices can be forgotten. With appropriate bounds
and duplicate handling, that discipline supports completeness
and sometimes a proof of optimality.

This chapter develops depth-first search, breadth-first
search, depth limits, iterative deepening, and branch-and-bound.
The methods differ in what they retain and which work they
select next. Their guarantees depend on the space being
searched and the objective being optimized.

Let b be an upper bound on branching, d the depth of a
shallowest goal, and m the greatest depth explored in a
bounded search tree. Depth counts transitions, not cost.
We use g for accumulated path cost. The distinction between
states and paths from [Week 1](01-models.md) remains essential:
a finite graph can unfold into an infinite tree of paths.

## Depth-first search

Depth-first search (DFS) pursues one branch until it reaches
a goal, a dead end, or a stated limit. It then backs up to an
ancestor with an unexplored successor. A recursive traversal
and an explicit last-in, first-out stack express this same
selection policy.

Suppose successors are tried in alphabetical order. In a
graph with S→A, S→B, A→C, C→G, and B→G, DFS follows
S, A, C, G and returns the three-edge route before considering
the two-edge route through B. Finding a goal is enough for
reachability. It does not establish that the route is shortest.

A recursive description keeps the current path and considers
one successor at a time:

```text
search(state, path):
    if goal(state): return a copy of path
    for each legal successor child in the chosen order:
        if child is not already on path:
            extend path with child
            result := search(child, path)
            remove child from path
            if result is a solution: return result
    return failure
```

The path-local test rejects cycles on the active route. Its
soundness here relies on memoryless legal futures and on
seeking one reachable goal: a cycle can be removed from a
successful route without changing what remains possible.
If a rule depends on earlier visits, that history belongs
in the state before applying this reasoning.

On a finite search tree, DFS eventually examines every node
unless it stops with a solution. Finite branching alone is
insufficient. An infinite chain below A can keep DFS busy
forever while a goal waits below B. A cycle can cause the
same failure in naive tree search over a finite graph.

For reachability in a finite graph, a global reached set
can prevent repeated expansion. Marking states when generated
avoids pushing several copies of the same state. Any one
arrival suffices for ordinary reachability, so suppressing
later arrivals preserves that task. It does not preserve the
task of enumerating all paths, and it does not by itself
solve minimum-cost search.

The memory difference matters. A tree DFS retaining pending
siblings uses O(bm) search records. Incremental successor
generation can reduce retained records toward the active
path plus generator state. A global reached set instead grows
to O(|V|); parent records add comparable storage. Copying an
entire path into every pending record adds still more memory.
A low-memory claim must identify the representation.

For a bounded tree with b>1, worst-case node count is O(b^m).
For a finite explicit graph, duplicate-aware DFS takes
O(|V|+|E|) time with adjacency lists and constant-time
reached-set operations. These descriptions measure different
inputs: an unfolded tree can contain many routes through
one graph vertex.

## Breadth-first search

Breadth-first search (BFS) examines paths in nondecreasing
depth. A first-in, first-out queue implements this order.
When a depth-k node generates children, they join the queue
behind all remaining depth-k nodes.

For graph reachability, mark states when first generated
and retain a parent link for reconstructing the result.

```text
frontier := queue containing the initial state
reached := set containing the initial state
while frontier is not empty:
    state := remove front of frontier
    if goal(state): return its reconstructed path
    for each successor child:
        if child is not in reached:
            add child to reached
            record state's parent link for child
            append child to frontier
return failure
```

In the earlier graph, removing S leaves [A,B]. Removing A
leaves [B,C]. Removing B discovers G, leaving [C,G].
When C is removed, G is already reached, so C does not enqueue
it again. Removing G returns S→B→G at depth two.
DFS's route through A has depth three.

Why is BFS shallowest-first? Initially only the root is
queued. Inductively, every generated child has depth one more
than its parent, and the FIFO rule leaves all shallower
queued nodes ahead of it. Thus no depth-(k+1) node is removed
before the remaining depth-k nodes. The first goal removed
has minimum depth.

Equal positive transition costs make minimum depth and
minimum path cost the same objective. Unequal costs do not.
A direct edge costing 20 is shallower than a two-edge route
costing 2, but is worse for a minimum-cost task.
[Week 4](04-best-first.md) replaces depth order with cost order.

With finite branching and a goal at finite depth, BFS is
complete: only finitely many nodes precede the goal's layer.
It may run forever without a goal in an infinite graph.
On a finite graph with a reached set, it terminates whether
or not a solution exists.

Goal-test timing changes the precise tree-space estimate.
The pseudocode tests on removal. Before the first goal at
depth d is removed, other depth-d nodes can generate children
at depth d+1. Its worst-case generated count and frontier
storage are therefore O(b^(d+1)), for b>1. The familiar
O(b^d) estimate applies to a version that tests for a goal
on generation and stops before expanding the goal layer.
Both conventions return a shallowest goal in ordinary BFS.
For explicit finite graphs the standard bounds remain
O(|V|+|E|) time and O(|V|) additional memory.

The practical difficulty is the frontier. DFS retains
alternatives along one path; BFS can retain nearly an entire
layer. A shallowest-route guarantee can become unusable if
the queue exhausts memory first.

## Depth-limited search

Depth-limited DFS refuses to expand a path beyond a specified
limit L. Test for a goal before applying the expansion cutoff,
so goals exactly at depth L remain eligible.

A useful result type distinguishes three outcomes:

- A solution was found.
- Complete failure: every eligible continuation was exhausted.
- Cutoff: some potentially useful continuation was excluded
  by the depth limit.

Cutoff does not establish that no solution exists. It says
that this limit did not settle the question. For example,
a search with L=2 cuts off the A→C→G route before G,
although another route may still find G through B.

For finite branching, the bounded traversal is finite.
It finds a goal at depth at most L if one exists and all
soundly eligible paths through that depth are considered.
For b>1 its tree work is O(b^L), with O(bL) retained records
in a version that stores pending siblings.

A global Boolean visited set is dangerous in a depth-limited
search. Imagine reaching X first at depth L, where no further
expansion is allowed. A later arrival at depth one may have
enough remaining depth to reach a goal through X. Discarding
that arrival because X was already seen loses the solution.
Use path-local cycle checking, or a depth-aware rule that
retains and acts on a better remaining-depth budget.

This is another example of dominance. An arrival is redundant
only when retained information covers its useful futures.
State equality alone does not establish that a shallower
arrival under a depth limit is redundant.

## Iterative deepening

Iterative deepening depth-first search, or IDDFS, runs
depth-limited DFS with limits 0, 1, 2, and so on.

```text
for limit := 0, 1, 2, ...:
    result := depth_limited_search(initial, limit)
    if result is a solution: return result
    if result is complete failure: return failure
```

Do not carry an ordinary visited set from one iteration to
the next. The larger limit makes previously excluded
continuations eligible. Caches require a separate proof
that their depth and path information supports safe reuse.

Every bounded iteration finishes with finite branching.
If a goal exists at finite depth d, the depth-d iteration
finds a goal after all shallower limits have failed.
Consequently IDDFS is complete for such goals and returns
a shallowest one. As with BFS, optimal path cost follows
only when every action has the same positive cost.

What does repeating the upper levels cost? In a regular
tree searched through depth d, the root is visited d+1
times, each depth-one node d times, and each depth-i node
d−i+1 times. The total is

**(d+1) + d·b + (d−1)·b² + … + b^d.**

For fixed b>1 this is O(b^d). Compared with one complete
traversal of the same layers, the ratio approaches b/(b−1).
For b=2 the limiting ratio is two; for b=10 it is about
1.11. This is a regular-tree calculation, not a promise
about every instance or every stopping point.

A chain behaves differently. With b=1, repeated limits
perform 1+2+…+(d+1) visits, giving quadratic work rather
than a constant-factor overhead over a single traversal.
The usual explanation that the deepest level dominates
depends on branching growth.

IDDFS uses O(bd) retained search records in the pending-sibling
implementation, plus state and path storage. Incremental
successor generation may use less. A global duplicate table
can again dominate this bound. IDDFS is particularly useful
when solution depth is unknown, costs are uniform, and a BFS
frontier would be too large.

If there is no solution in an infinite space, iterations can
continue forever. If a finite graph uses path-local cycle
checking, only finitely many simple paths exist; a sufficiently
large limit can exhaust them and return complete failure.
The cycle policy determines whether that failure certificate
will eventually be available.

## Branch-and-bound

Branch-and-bound adds optimization to systematic exploration.
Maintain an **incumbent**, a complete feasible solution of
cost U. Since the true optimum C* cannot exceed a known
feasible cost, C*≤U.

For a partial path n, let L(n) lower-bound the cost of every
complete solution extending it. If L(n)≥U, that branch cannot
strictly improve the incumbent. It can be pruned when finding
one optimal answer is enough. To enumerate all optimal ties,
equality requires different treatment.

For nonnegative additive edge costs, accumulated path cost
g(n) is already a lower bound. An admissible remaining-cost
estimate h(n) strengthens it to L(n)=g(n)+h(n).
An estimate that sometimes overstates remaining cost can
discard an optimal branch; optimism is a correctness condition.

```text
incumbent := none
U := infinity

explore(path, g):
    state := last state on path
    if goal(state):
        if g < U:
            retain a copy of path as incumbent
            U := g
        return
    if lower_bound(path, g) >= U: return
    for each eligible successor child:
        extend path, explore it, and restore path
```

The bound applies to this path's possible completions.
A general CSP optimization model may use a bound on the
partial assignment's eventual objective instead of a path
cost. In either setting, the bound must match the objective
and retained information.

Suppose the first complete route costs 12. Install U=12.
Another partial route has accumulated cost 5 and a justified
total lower bound of 9. It remains eligible: it might finish
at cost 10. A branch with total lower bound 12 can be pruned.
When the cost-10 route is found, update U=10 and prune future
branches with bounds at least 10.

Calling a candidate promising supplies no upper bound.
Only a complete feasible answer supplies U. Likewise,
inventing a bound of 13 for the branch that actually finishes
at 10 would make the pruning unsound.

The finite-tree correctness argument is direct. Each pruned
branch cannot improve the current feasible incumbent. Since
later incumbents only improve, that discarded branch cannot
hide a solution better than the final incumbent either.
Every unpruned branch is eventually explored. At exhaustion,
no cheaper solution remains. If there is no solution,
finite exhaustive traversal establishes failure.

Depth-first branch-and-bound can use little search memory
and often obtains an incumbent early. Best-bound order
instead selects the smallest L from a frontier, retaining
more alternatives. Ordering affects effort and early answers;
the pruning argument depends on valid bounds and sufficient
coverage, not on one mandatory ordering.

Infinite spaces need care. Before any incumbent is found,
ordinary DFS can follow an infinite branch and miss a goal.
After a finite incumbent exists, finite branching and a fixed
positive lower edge-cost bound ε imply that any improving
path has depth below U/ε. With nonnegative h, all paths whose
bounds remain below U lie inside that finite-depth region.
Exhaustive bounded exploration can then establish optimality.

Zero-cost paths in an infinite space break that argument:
arbitrarily long paths can remain under the same bound.
Negative edges also invalidate g as a lower bound and can
create cycles with no finite optimum. A different cost model
requires a different proof.

## Choosing an exploration policy

| Need | Starting method | Main qualification |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Any reachable goal, little retained work | DFS | Bound or control infinite branches and cycles |
| Fewest transitions | BFS | A complete layer can consume much memory |
| Known depth budget | Depth-limited DFS | Cutoff is not failure |
| Unknown depth, uniform costs, limited memory | IDDFS | Regeneration costs depend on branching |
| Minimum objective with feasible candidates | Branch-and-bound | Bounds must be sound and coverage sufficient |

These choices express resource and guarantee tradeoffs.
A reached set changes memory use. A depth limit changes
what a repeated arrival can still accomplish. An incumbent
changes which branches can improve the answer. Treat each
detail as part of the algorithm.

The next chapter orders alternatives by path cost and
heuristic estimates. It retains the same obligation:
explain why a discarded arrival or pruned branch cannot
change the required answer.

## Further reading

- Korf, [“Depth-First Iterative-Deepening: An Optimal
  Admissible Tree Search”](https://doi.org/10.1016/0004-3702(85)90084-0)
  (1985). Develops iterative deepening and its search-cost
  analysis; the cost-bounded form returns in Week 5.
- Korf, [“A Complete Anytime Algorithm for Number
  Partitioning”](https://web.cecs.pdx.edu/bart/cs510cs/papers/korf-ckk.pdf)
  (1998). Connects strong early heuristic answers with
  complete exploration and an eventual optimality proof.

# Week 4: Best-First Search

Depth-first and breadth-first search choose work by a
structural rule. Best-first search instead assigns each
frontier entry a priority and removes one with minimum
priority. The score can represent cost already paid, estimated
cost still to come, or both. Those choices define different
algorithms with different guarantees.

We use g for a path's accumulated cost, h for an estimate of
remaining cost, and h* for the true cheapest remaining cost.
All edge costs are nonnegative. Heuristics are nonnegative
and zero at goals. An admissible heuristic satisfies h≤h*.
A consistent heuristic additionally satisfies
h(s)≤c(s,t)+h(t) on every edge s→t.

A queue entry represents a path to a state, not just the
state itself. Two entries for one state can have different
costs. Handling that difference correctly is as important
as selecting the priority formula.

## One queue, three priorities

| Method | Priority | What it favors |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Uniform-cost search | g | Cheapest discovered path prefix |
| Greedy best-first search | h | Smallest estimated remaining cost |
| A* | g+h | Smallest estimated total solution cost |

A tie-break rule selects among equal priorities. It affects
traces and performance. We specify ties where needed in a
worked example; the basic cost proofs permit any rule that
does not indefinitely postpone required work.

Uniform-cost search, abbreviated UCS, is the search
interpretation of Dijkstra's shortest-path algorithm.
A* reduces to UCS when h is zero everywhere. Greedy search
with h=0 instead makes all entries tie. It does not become
UCS unless some additional rule explicitly orders by g.

A priority is a selection rule. It is not automatically a
lower bound or a certificate. Greedy h omits the path cost.
Weighted priorities studied later can deliberately exceed a
valid completion-cost lower bound. Give each score a meaning
before using it in a proof.

## Arrivals, improvements, and stale entries

Keep a table best_g[s] recording the least cost discovered
for state s. A new path is worth enqueuing when its cost
strictly improves that record. Initialize best_g[start]=0;
other states have no known cost, conventionally infinity.

Many queues make insertion easier than changing the key of
an existing entry. A **lazy update** simply inserts the
improved path and leaves the old entry in the queue.
On removal, compare the stored cost with current best_g.
An outdated entry is **stale** and must be skipped.

```text
best_g[start] := 0
insert an entry for start with g=0 and its priority

while the queue is not empty:
    entry := remove a minimum-priority entry
    s := entry.state
    if entry.g != best_g[s]: continue
    if goal(s): return the path represented by entry

    for each edge s→t of cost c:
        candidate := entry.g + c
        if t has no recorded cost or candidate < best_g[t]:
            best_g[t] := candidate
            create a path entry for t, linked to entry
            insert it with the chosen priority
return failure
```

Each path entry here has an immutable parent-entry link.
Reconstruction therefore follows the exact route represented
by the selected entry. A compact implementation may instead
maintain state-based predecessor records, but it must ensure
that reconstruction and the reported cost remain consistent
when records change.

Strict improvement suppresses equal-cost duplicates,
including repeated travel around a zero-cost cycle.
The algorithm seeks one solution path. Enumerating all
optimal paths needs extra predecessor information and a
different treatment of ties.

This general loop has no permanent closed set. A state can
be expanded again after a strict cost improvement.
For UCS, a nonstale expansion already has optimal g, so
reopening is unnecessary under nonnegative costs.
For A*, that conclusion requires consistency; admissibility
alone does not provide it.

## Uniform-cost search

UCS chooses minimum g. Suppose S has a direct edge to goal G
costing 10, and an edge to A costing 1, followed by A→G
costing 1. Expanding S generates a goal, but that goal is
not yet a reason to stop.

The queue first contains A at cost 1 and G at cost 10.
Removing A discovers a better G entry at cost 2.
That entry is removed next and returns S→A→G.
The old cost-10 entry is stale if it is ever examined.

This example motivates accepting a goal on a nonstale
minimum removal, rather than on generation. Generating a
goal establishes a feasible upper bound. It does not
establish that all cheaper routes have been ruled out.

The optimality argument considers a supposedly cheaper
solution. Suppose UCS removes a goal costing C, while an
optimal route costs C*<C. Along that route, retain the first
prefix whose optimal-cost arrival has not yet been expanded.
Its predecessor's optimal arrival has already been expanded,
so this prefix, or an equally good arrival, remains eligible
in the queue. Its cost is at most C*. It must precede a
cost-C goal, contradicting the minimum-g selection.

This argument also explains why a Boolean visited flag on
generation is wrong for weighted paths. The first generated
route to G cost 10. Marking G permanently visited at that
moment would block the later improvement to 2.

On a finite graph, nonnegative costs and strict best-g
improvements give termination and an optimal answer whenever
a goal is reachable. If no goal is reachable, the finite
search is exhausted and reports failure.

On an infinite graph, a useful sufficient condition is finite
branching, a finite-cost solution, and a fixed positive lower
bound ε on every edge cost. A path costing at most C then
has depth at most C/ε. Only finitely many paths can precede
the goal's cost contour.

Merely positive costs are insufficient. Costs can shrink
along an infinite path so their sum stays below a goal's cost.
Zero-cost edges can likewise create infinitely many distinct
cost-zero states. An infinite low-cost region can delay the
goal forever.

Negative edges invalidate UCS's finalization argument.
A route expanded at cost 5 might later be improved through
an as-yet-unseen negative edge. Negative cycles can make a
finite minimum undefined. Such models need other algorithms.

For an explicit graph with adjacency lists, a binary heap
with one active record per vertex gives the familiar
O((|V|+|E|) log |V|) bound. A lazy queue can hold O(|E|)
records and has a corresponding logarithmic queue cost.
The distinction matters for multigraphs and actual memory
accounting. In implicit problems, exponentially many states
may fit below the optimal cost contour.

## Greedy best-first search

Greedy best-first search chooses minimum h, ignoring g.
It asks which state appears closest to a goal, regardless
of the expense of getting there.

Consider S→A costing 8 and A→G costing 1, versus S→B
costing 1 and B→G costing 4. Set h(A)=0, h(B)=3, and
h(G)=0. Greedy chooses A, then the goal it generates,
returning cost 9. The alternative costs 5.

Both estimates are admissible: A has true remaining cost 1,
and B has true remaining cost 4. Even setting h(S)=0 makes
this example consistent. Neither property makes greedy
search cost-optimal; its priority omits accumulated cost.

A finite graph can be searched completely with adequate
duplicate control. An infinite graph can defeat greedy
search even with finite branching and positive costs:
an infinite sequence of attractive estimates can keep
outranking a reachable goal elsewhere.

Greedy search is useful when early feasibility matters and
the estimate effectively guides the tested problem family.
A returned route is a valid answer to reachability.
Its path cost has no general approximation guarantee.
Calling the estimate admissible does not change that fact.

This distinction is easy to lose because UCS, greedy search,
and A* can share almost all their implementation machinery.
Changing one priority formula changes the mathematical
reason the first removed goal should be accepted.

## A* and admissible lower bounds

A* chooses minimum f=g+h. Since h is admissible,
g+h lower-bounds the cost of every completion of this
particular path. A* combines the price already paid with
an optimistic estimate of what remains.

Let C* be the optimal solution cost. While an optimal route
has not been completed, a correctly maintained frontier
contains an eligible prefix of an optimal route with its
optimal prefix cost. For that prefix, g+h≤C*.

Now suppose A* removes a suboptimal goal costing C>C*.
Its priority is C because h(goal)=0. The optimal prefix
has a strictly smaller priority, contradicting minimum-f
selection. Thus the removed goal is optimal.

The frontier-prefix claim is the substance of the proof.
It can fail if the implementation throws away a useful
better arrival. A* with an admissible heuristic therefore
needs correct strict-g updates and, when necessary, reopening.
An algorithm name alone does not provide the guarantee.

On finite graphs, the loop above terminates under the stated
nonnegative-cost assumptions. On infinite spaces, finite
branching and costs bounded below by ε>0 again provide a
useful sufficient condition: nonnegative h makes g≤f,
so every entry with f≤C* has bounded depth.
Admissibility by itself does not ensure finite progress
through infinitely many cheap states.

A heuristic may underestimate by a large amount and remain
admissible. That can make A* explore almost as much as UCS.
An overestimate can focus work well in practice but removes
this optimality proof. [Week 10](10-frontiers.md) gives a
controlled way to trade solution quality for search order.

## Consistency and reopening

Consistency supplies a relation between neighbors:

**h(s) ≤ c(s,t)+h(t).**

Adding g(s) shows that f cannot decrease along a path:
g(s)+h(s)≤g(s)+c(s,t)+h(t).
With consistent h, a state's first nonstale A* expansion has
its least possible path cost. A permanent closed set can
therefore finalize it.

Consistency also implies admissibility for states with a
finite route to a goal, when goal estimates are zero.
Apply the inequality repeatedly along any such route;
the intermediate h terms cancel and leave h(s) no greater
than that route's cost. Taking a cheapest route gives h≤h*.

The converse is false. An admissible heuristic can make
an estimate drop abruptly across a cheap edge.
A* can then expand a state through an expensive route before
discovering a cheaper one.

[![The graph has S→A cost 3, S→B cost 1, B→A cost 1, and A→G cost 3; heuristic values are 5 at S, 4 at B, and 0 at A and G.](figures/reopening.svg)](figures/reopening.svg)

In this original example, the true remaining costs are
5 at S, 4 at B, 3 at A, and 0 at G.
The displayed heuristic is admissible. It is inconsistent
on B→A because 4 is greater than 1+0.

| Removed entry | Work performed |
| --- | --- |
| S, g=0, f=5 | Insert A at g=3,f=3 and B at g=1,f=5 |
| A, g=3, f=3 | Insert G at g=6,f=6 |
| B, g=1, f=5 | Improve A to g=2,f=2 |
| A, g=2, f=2 | Improve G to g=5,f=5 |
| G, g=5, f=5 | Return S→B→A→G, cost 5 |

A must be expanded twice. A version that permanently closes
A after its first expansion can instead return cost 6.
The strict-improvement loop permits the reopening naturally:
the new A record is eligible even though an older A record
was expanded.

The stale cost-6 goal is harmless because the current
cost-5 goal is removed first. More generally, skip stale
records before using them for expansion or termination.
Queue membership alone does not establish that a stored
path still represents the best discovered arrival.

## Heuristic strength and practical cost

Suppose h₂(s)≥h₁(s) everywhere and both are admissible.
Then h₂ is said to dominate h₁. It supplies at least as
tight a lower bound at every state. Maximum combination
can produce such improvements without double-counting.

This does not mean a stronger heuristic is automatically
faster. Computing it may cost more. Ties on the optimal
f contour, inconsistent estimates and repeated expansions,
preprocessing, and table lookups all affect actual work.
Measure runtime as well as node counts.

Nor does heuristic guidance eliminate A*'s frontier storage.
Keys, path entries, best-g records, queue slack, and stale
entries can grow large. An excellent estimate may make a
particular instance easy while another instance still
exhausts memory.

[Week 5](05-heuristics.md) explains how to construct lower
bounds by relaxation and abstraction, combine estimates
safely, and trade repeated work for reduced retained memory.
The common basis is the meaning of g+h as a bound.
The algorithms differ in how much of the frontier they
keep available.

## Further reading

- Dijkstra, [“A Note on Two Problems in Connexion with
  Graphs”](https://doi.org/10.1007/BF01386390) (1959).
  The shortest-path method underlying UCS.
- Hart, Nilsson, and Raphael,
  [“A Formal Basis for the Heuristic Determination of
  Minimum Cost Paths”](https://doi.org/10.1109/TSSC.1968.300136)
  (1968). The foundational formal treatment of A*.
- Dechter and Pearl,
  [“Generalized Best-First Search Strategies and the
  Optimality of A*”](https://doi.org/10.1145/3828.3830)
  (1985). Develops the conditions behind stronger claims
  about best-first search and efficiency.

# Week 5: Heuristics and Limited Memory

[Week 4](04-best-first.md) established why A* uses g+h:
accumulated cost plus an admissible estimate lower-bounds
the cost of completing a path. We now ask where useful
estimates come from and what to do when the frontier does
not fit in memory.

A heuristic h is admissible when 0≤h(s)≤h*(s), where h*
is the true cheapest remaining cost. At goals h=0.
A zero heuristic is admissible but supplies little guidance.
The design task is to obtain a stronger lower bound without
spending more time or memory than the resulting search saves.

## Relaxing the problem

A **relaxation** makes the problem easier in a controlled way.
Every original solution must remain a permitted relaxed
solution, with no greater cost. The relaxed optimum then
cannot exceed the original optimum.

If h_R(s) is the exact relaxed optimum from s, it follows
that h_R(s)≤h*(s). This is an admissibility argument.
The relaxed problem may have physically impossible plans;
that is acceptable because their costs are used as optimistic
bounds, not returned as executable answers.

The word “exact” matters. Finding one relaxed solution
provides an upper bound on the relaxed optimum. That value
need not lower-bound the original optimum. An approximation
to the relaxed optimum requires its own lower-bound argument
before it can safely guide optimal A* pruning.

For a sliding-tile puzzle, a legal unit-cost action moves
one numbered tile into the adjacent blank. Ignore interference
between numbered tiles and ask how many grid steps each tile
needs to reach its goal cell. A tile at row r and column c,
with goal row r_g and column c_g, needs at least

**|r−r_g| + |c−c_g|**

moves of that tile. Summing these distances for the numbered
tiles gives **Manhattan distance**. Do not include the blank.

The sum is admissible because each legal action moves exactly
one numbered tile by one grid step. A real solution must pay
for every tile's required displacement. Tiles blocking one
another can add moves, but cannot remove that necessary work.

[![The current board is 1,2,3 / 4,blank,6 / 7,5,8. The goal is 1,2,3 / 4,5,6 / 7,8,blank. Tiles 5 and 8 each need one step, giving Manhattan distance 2.](figures/manhattan.svg)](figures/manhattan.svg)

Here only tiles 5 and 8 are displaced. Move 5 upward into
the blank, then 8 leftward into the new blank. The estimate
2 equals the true solution cost in this instance.
Other configurations can require detours that the independent
tile calculation omits.

Manhattan distance is also consistent for this unit-cost
puzzle. One move changes the distance of only the moved
tile, by one. The estimate cannot drop by more than that
move's cost. This extra property supports the finalization
rule discussed in Week 4.

## Combining lower bounds

Suppose h₁ and h₂ are admissible for the same remaining-cost
objective. Their maximum is admissible:

**h_max(s)=max(h₁(s),h₂(s)).**

Each component is no larger than h*, so their maximum is
no larger either. Maximum combination uses whichever bound
is stronger at the current state.

Their sum is not automatically safe. If both components
count the same necessary move, adding them counts that move
twice. Two estimates of one can sum to two even when one
action reaches the goal. The estimates were individually
admissible; the combination is not.

Addition becomes safe through **cost partitioning**.
For every real action a, assign nonnegative component
costs c_i(a) such that their sum is no greater than c(a).
Each component problem must admit a projection of every
real solution with those assigned costs.

Take any real solution. Its projection in component i
costs at least that component's optimal value h_i.
Summing these values charges no more than the real path's
total cost, by the per-action condition. This is true for
every real solution, including an optimal one. Therefore
the sum of the h_i values remains admissible.

This is the same accounting principle used for scheduling
bounds in [Week 8](08-engineering.md). Different explanations
of necessary work may overlap. Their maximum is often safe;
their sum requires evidence that the costs do not overlap.

## Pattern databases

A **pattern database** stores exact remaining costs for
a simplified, abstract state space. At search time, map the
concrete state to its abstract state and look up the result.
The admissibility proof belongs to the abstraction: a
concrete solution must project to an abstract solution of
no greater cost.

In a tile puzzle, a pattern retains the positions of a
selected group of tiles and the information needed for
legal abstract moves, often including the blank. Other
tiles become indistinguishable background. A table can be
built by searching backward from abstract goals.

A larger pattern preserves more tile interactions. It can
give a stronger estimate while requiring much more storage
and preprocessing. State ranking maps each abstract
configuration to a table index; it must preserve the intended
identity, rather than accidentally merging different cases.

For additive databases, divide numbered tiles into disjoint
groups. Assign a real move's unit cost to the group containing
the tile moved. In every other group's abstract problem,
that move costs zero. Across all groups, one real move is
charged exactly once.

Compute each abstract shortest-path table using those costs
and add the lookups. Each real plan projects to every
component, and the summed charges do not exceed its cost.
Interactions among tiles within a group can make this
stronger than independent Manhattan distances.

Disjoint tile names alone are not sufficient. If several
tables each charge the full cost of a shared action, their
sum may overestimate. Explain the abstract transitions and
the cost assignment together.

Zero-cost abstract moves also affect construction.
Ordinary FIFO BFS is not generally a shortest-path algorithm
for mixed zero/one costs. Dijkstra or a suitable zero/one
queue procedure respects that cost model. Using the wrong
precomputation algorithm can corrupt the heuristic before
the main search begins.

The total memory budget must include these tables.
An algorithm with a tiny active search stack can still use
gigabytes of heuristic data. Report preprocessing time,
table size, lookup cost, and whether reuse across instances
justifies that investment.

## IDA*: iterative deepening on cost estimates

Iterative deepening A*, or **IDA***, replaces a retained
best-first frontier with a sequence of depth-first traversals.
Each traversal permits only paths whose f=g+h is no greater
than a threshold B.

Start with B=h(start). When a node exceeds the threshold,
record its f value and backtrack. After an unsuccessful
iteration, use the smallest exceeded f as the next threshold.
Do not simply add one: costs and estimates may be fractional,
irregular, or separated by large gaps.

```text
current_path := [start]
bound := h(start)
repeat:
    next_bound := infinity
    result := visit(start, g=0, bound, current_path)
    if result is a solution: return result
    if next_bound = infinity: return failure
    bound := next_bound

visit(state, g, bound, path):
    f := g + h(state)
    if f > bound:
        next_bound := min(next_bound, f)
        return failure
    if goal(state): return a copy of the current path
    for each successor not already on path:
        extend path, recurse with its cost, and restore path
        if recursion found a solution: return it
    return failure
```

The shared next_bound is reset once per iteration.
Test f before accepting a goal, so a goal outside the current
cost threshold cannot bypass the bound. Preserve a copy of
the successful path before restoring mutable path storage.

Consider S→A and S→B, each costing 1. A leads to goal G_A
with cost 5; B leads to G_B with cost 2.
Set h(S)=2, h(A)=5, h(B)=1, and h=0 at both goals.
The best real solution costs 3 through B.

With A tried first and bound 2, A has f=6 and is cut off.
B has f=2 and is expanded, but its goal has f=3 and is cut
off. The next threshold is min(6,3)=3.
The second iteration still rejects A and reaches G_B at cost
3. It does not waste passes at thresholds unrelated to an
observed boundary.

Why is this optimal? On an optimal route, every path prefix
has admissible f≤C*. If an iteration below C* fails, the
first excluded prefix on that route offers an exceeded
value no greater than C*. The next threshold therefore
need not jump above C*. Once a goal is accepted, its cost
equals its f and cannot exceed C*.

That argument also needs finite progress. With finite
branching, nonnegative h, and edge costs bounded below
by ε>0, a traversal under B reaches depth at most B/ε.
There are only finitely many paths inside the optimal
cost contour, so the thresholds cannot postpone a finite-cost
optimal goal through infinitely many smaller boundary values.

For a finite graph with path-local cycle checking,
nonnegative costs can suffice without a positive ε:
only finitely many simple paths exist. On an infinite
graph, zero costs or arbitrarily small positive costs can
defeat termination of one bounded traversal.

## What IDA* retains

A path-local cycle set rejects states already on the active
route. It permits the same state on other routes and in
later iterations. A global visited set carried between
iterations would suppress work made newly eligible by a
larger threshold. A transposition cache needs cost-, depth-,
and threshold-aware reasoning.

Let D be the greatest depth actually reached during the
run. With incrementally generated successors and constant-size
state records, IDA* can use O(D) search records.
Materializing all siblings at each level instead gives
O(bD). Neither figure includes pattern databases or optional
duplicate tables.

D need not equal the shallowest goal depth. Unequal costs
and depth-first ordering can send the traversal deeply into
a branch before it returns a shallower goal. Avoid calling
all depth-based memory bounds O(d) without saying which
depth d measures.

The memory saving comes from regeneration. Each threshold
starts over. A weak heuristic, irregular costs, or many
closely spaced boundary values can produce substantial
repeated work. IDA* is attractive when the frontier is the
limiting resource and lower bounds prune enough of the tree
to compensate for discarded history.

## Recursive best-first search

**Recursive best-first search**, or RBFS, retains more
information about nearby alternatives. It descends through
the best current child while remembering the best competitor
outside that branch. When the chosen branch becomes more
expensive than that competitor, it backs up a summary and
changes direction.

Each node has a backed-up value F. At the root,
F=h(start). Initialize a generated child's value as

**F(child)=max(F(parent), g(child)+h(child)).**

The maximum prevents estimates from decreasing along the
active path, even when h is inconsistent. The inherited value
is a lower bound already established for that branch's
possible completions.

At a node, sort children by F. Recurse into the best child
with a limit equal to the smaller of the inherited limit
and the second-best child's F. If the chosen branch later
exceeds that limit, the recursive call returns its revised
F. Store the summary and compare alternatives again.

```text
RBFS(node, limit):
    if node is a goal: return solution, F(node)
    generate children excluding active-path cycles
    initialize each child's F
    if no children exist: return failure, infinity
    repeat:
        choose best and second-best children by F
        if F(best) = infinity or F(best) > limit:
            return failure, F(best)
        alternative := F(second-best), or infinity if absent
        result, revised := RBFS(best, min(limit, alternative))
        F(best) := revised
        if result is a solution: return result, revised
```

The infinity test is necessary. When the best branch is
exhausted and the limit is also infinity, the comparison
infinity>infinity is false. Without the explicit exhaustion
case, an implementation can recurse repeatedly into work
already proved fruitless.

For a small example, suppose two children have F values
4 and 7, and the inherited limit is 10.
RBFS explores the first with limit 7. If that branch reports
a new bound of 9, the children now rank 7 and 9.
The other branch is explored with limit 9.
The algorithm remembers that the first branch costs at
least 9, rather than remembering all its descendants.

Stored sibling bounds make this more responsive than
restarting from the root at every global threshold.
They do not preserve the complete frontier. When an old
branch becomes best again, forgotten descendants must be
regenerated. Repeated switching can make total time much
larger than A*'s.

RBFS retains up to b child records at each of D active
levels, giving O(bD) search records under the stated
constant-record assumption. It is linear in depth when
branching is treated as bounded. Heuristic tables and large
concrete states remain additional costs.

With admissible estimates and appropriate finite-search
conditions, the backed-up bounds preserve the possibility
of an optimal route while alternatives are reordered.
As with IDA*, finite branching and a positive lower cost
bound provide useful conditions for finite progress in
potentially infinite spaces. Path-cycle checking avoids
cyclic active routes; it does not eliminate every repeated
state across different routes.

## Choosing what to remember

A* keeps a global frontier and avoids much regeneration.
IDA* keeps a path and repeats cost-bounded traversals.
RBFS keeps a path plus nearby sibling summaries, forgetting
detailed descendants when it backs out.

All three use the same lower-bound idea. Their different
memory policies decide how much previously discovered
structure remains immediately available. There is no
universal winner: heuristic strength, table storage,
duplicate frequency, successor cost, and available memory
all influence the practical tradeoff.

The next chapter changes strategy more substantially.
Local search keeps complete candidates and repairs them,
rather than retaining a systematic account of every
unexplored branch.

## Further reading

- Korf and Felner,
  [“Disjoint Pattern Database Heuristics”](https://doi.org/10.1016/S0004-3702(01)00092-3)
  (2002). Explains additive abstraction heuristics and
  the accounting needed to combine them safely.
- Korf, [“Depth-First Iterative-Deepening: An Optimal
  Admissible Tree Search”](https://doi.org/10.1016/0004-3702(85)90084-0)
  (1985). The foundational cost-bounded iterative-deepening
  result behind IDA*.
- Korf, [“Linear-Space Best-First Search”](https://doi.org/10.1016/0004-3702(93)90045-D)
  (1993). Develops RBFS and the tradeoff between retained
  bounds, memory, and regeneration.

# Week 9: Adversarial Search

A pathfinder chooses actions in a world whose transitions
follow its model. A game player also faces another
decision-maker who chooses replies. A promising leaf is
not enough: the opponent may choose a different continuation.

This chapter studies deterministic, perfect-information,
two-player, zero-sum games with alternating turns.
Actions have known results, both players observe the
rule-relevant situation, and one player's gain is the
other's loss. Call the player at the root MAX and its
opponent MIN. These names stay fixed throughout the search.
All utilities are measured from MAX's perspective.

The goal is to choose a move with a strong guaranteed outcome
against an opponent who also chooses well. We first define
that outcome precisely, then explain how to obtain it with
less work and how practical depth limits change its meaning.

## States, turns, and terminal outcomes

A game state includes the side to move and every other fact
that affects future rules or outcomes. A chess board alone
omits castling rights, en-passant rights, and draw-relevant
history. States that look identical on the board can have
different legal futures.

Let A(s) be legal actions, T(s,a) the deterministic resulting
state, and U(s) the utility of a terminal state to MAX.
For a simple win/draw/loss game, use +1, 0, and −1.
Some games instead have numeric terminal scores.

Assume initially that the explored game tree is finite.
Games with cycles need explicit repetition or draw rules,
a bounded horizon, or another termination argument.
Recursing forever on repeated positions does not solve them.

A path represents one possible play sequence.
Different sequences can reach the same state, creating
**transpositions**. Their reuse is safe only when the
state includes everything needed for the rules and the
stored result answers the current search question.

Hidden information requires a different model. A public
board and unknown private cards do not give the player
one known perfect-information state. Likewise, a die roll
is a chance event rather than a strategic choice.
We return briefly to chance after deterministic games.

## Minimax

The **minimax value** uses the same utility scale at every
depth:

- At a terminal state, V(s)=U(s).
- At a MAX state, V(s) is the maximum child value.
- At a MIN state, V(s) is the minimum child value.

MAX chooses its most favorable child; MIN chooses the child
least favorable to MAX. Apply the recurrence upward from
leaves to obtain the root value. A root action attaining
that value is an optimal choice under this model.

Consider a MAX root with moves North and South.
After North, MIN chooses terminal utilities 3 or 5.
After South, MIN chooses 2 or 9.

North has value min(3,5)=3.
South has value min(2,9)=2.
MAX chooses North and guarantees value 3.

The largest leaf is 9, but it requires MIN to cooperate.
Choosing a route to that leaf treats the opponent's action
as if MAX controlled it. Minimax instead respects who makes
each choice.

[![MAX chooses between North, whose MIN replies have utilities 3 and 5, and South, whose replies have utilities 2 and 9. North has value 3; South is bounded above by 2 after its first reply, allowing the utility-9 reply to be pruned.](figures/alpha-beta.svg)](figures/alpha-beta.svg)

The recurrence is correct by induction on remaining depth.
At leaves, the assigned utilities are the rules of the model.
If child values correctly represent optimal continuation,
taking the maximum or minimum represents the current player's
best available action. That establishes the parent value.
Applying this step to the root establishes minimax.

For maximum branching b>1 and horizon D, full-width work is
O(b^D) in the worst case. With incrementally generated
successors, the active traversal can retain O(D) records;
storing all siblings at every level gives O(bD).
Concrete state sizes and transposition tables add storage.

One **ply** is one player's move. Increasing a horizon by
one ply can multiply tree size by roughly the branching
factor. This growth motivates pruning even before considering
more complicated evaluators.

## Alpha-beta pruning

**Alpha-beta search** obtains the same minimax root value
while sometimes leaving subtrees unexplored.

Alpha, α, represents a lower bound already available to MAX
through choices along the current ancestry. Beta, β,
represents a corresponding upper bound imposed by MIN.
At a MAX node, improve the local best value and raise α.
At a MIN node, improve the local minimum and lower β.
When α≥β, further children cannot improve the relevant
ancestor's decision.

Start the root with α=−∞ and β=∞.
Search North first. Its first reply has value 3, lowering
North's β to 3. Its second reply is 5, so North remains 3.
The root can now choose an action worth 3 and raises α to 3.

Search South with inherited α=3. Its first reply is 2,
lowering β to 2. Since 2≤3, stop: MIN can hold South to
at most 2, while MAX already has North worth 3.
The utility-9 leaf need not be examined.

This is a bound argument, not a prediction that the unseen
leaf is bad. At a MIN node, finding one sufficiently low
child establishes an upper bound on the node's value:
additional children can only keep or lower that minimum.
At a MAX node, finding one sufficiently high child
establishes a lower bound by the symmetric argument.

The cutoff includes equality. If an alternative cannot
improve on a known value, it can be skipped when the task
is to find one optimal action. Enumerating all tied optimal
actions, or applying a secondary preference among them,
requires preserving more information. A value-preserving
cutoff need not preserve every tied line.

An interior-node return following a cutoff may be a bound
rather than an exact value. In the example, searching only
South's first child establishes V(South)≤2.
It does not establish equality unless its other children
are also accounted for. The root choice is nevertheless
exact because South cannot defeat North.

## Move ordering

Alpha-beta's worst-case work remains O(b^D). With ideal
ordering in a regular tree, the leaf count can be on the
order of b^(D/2). This is an idealized bound; an actual
tree's shape, move order, and horizon determine its savings.

Try good moves early to tighten bounds sooner.
A previous iteration's best move, tactical domain knowledge,
or a stored transposition move can supply an ordering hint.
The hint does not need to prove anything about the value:
a poor ordering increases work without changing the
full-width minimax result.

Permanently deleting a move because it looks unpromising
is different. Unless a sound pruning argument applies,
that deletion changes the game being searched.
Separating ordering hints from proof-bearing cutoffs is
the same discipline used for lower bounds in path search.

Ties should be resolved consistently when tracing or
benchmarking an implementation. Different tied orders can
create different cutoff patterns even while the final
root value remains identical.

## Depth limits and evaluation

Large games cannot usually be searched to terminal states.
At a chosen horizon, replace unfinished leaves with an
evaluation E(s), also from MAX's perspective.
The recurrence then computes minimax for this truncated
tree, not the actual game value.

An evaluator can combine features such as material,
mobility, threats, and positional control.
Larger scores must always favor MAX.
A fixed-perspective implementation maximizes at MAX nodes
and minimizes at MIN nodes; it does not arbitrarily negate
the evaluator on alternate calls.

Negamax is another valid convention for suitable zero-sum
games. It changes perspective and negates returned values
at turns. Mixing negamax sign rules with a fixed-MAX
evaluator produces plausible but incorrect decisions.
Choose one convention and keep terminal and heuristic
scores consistent with it.

Terminal scores need an appropriate range. If every
nonterminal estimate lies between −100 and 100, a terminal
MAX win can be assigned a larger score than 100.
Without such separation, an estimated favorable position
can outrank a known win.

A **horizon effect** occurs when a consequence falls just
beyond the boundary. A position may look favorable one ply
before an unavoidable capture. Searching deeper or extending
unstable positions can expose that consequence, but costs
more work and does not eliminate every horizon problem.

A **quiescence search** continues selected tactical
continuations instead of immediately applying a static
evaluation in an unstable position. Its move selection and
termination rules become part of the search semantics.
It is not a proof of full-game optimality.

A deeper search can also expose an evaluator's biases.
Depth alone does not guarantee stronger play if the model,
terminal handling, or evaluation is wrong.
Use small tactical examples and independently computed
trees to distinguish rule bugs from evaluation weaknesses.

## Iterative deepening under a deadline

Search successively to horizons 1, 2, 3, and so on.
Early iterations supply a completed answer and improve
move ordering for later iterations. The previous best root
move is tried first; useful continuation moves can guide
the rest of the tree.

Keep the result of the last fully completed iteration.
If a deadline interrupts the next iteration, returning a
partially updated root result can unfairly compare a fully
searched move with an unfinished competitor.
A legal fallback move should exist even before depth one
finishes.

The **principal variation** is the search's current preferred
line: MAX's choice, MIN's preferred reply, and so on.
It explains the model's forecast, not a promise that actual
play will follow that line.

This is an anytime mechanism in the practical sense of
having an answer available under interruption.
Unlike a monotonically improving optimization incumbent,
deeper heuristic minimax values need not improve monotonically.
A horizon can reveal a threat or change which evaluation
features dominate.

Record the completed horizon and search semantics with a
result. “Searched to depth eight” is ambiguous if selective
extensions or reductions make different branches reach
different effective horizons.

## Transposition tables

A **transposition table** stores information from earlier
searches of the same state. An entry can include its key,
remaining horizon, value, bound type, and suggested move.

Exact state comparison provides collision-safe identity.
A compact fingerprint instead introduces a probabilistic
tradeoff. Two hashes that happen to agree do not constitute
a mathematical proof of state equality. The representation
must also distinguish turn, rights, and relevant history.

The bound types are:

| Type | Meaning for the compatible query |
| --- | --- |
| EXACT | V equals the stored value |
| LOWER | V is at least the stored value |
| UPPER | V is at most the stored value |

A cutoff at a MAX node can establish a LOWER bound;
a cutoff at a MIN node can establish an UPPER bound.
Storing every return as EXACT can corrupt later decisions.

For a compatible query, an EXACT entry can be returned
directly. A LOWER entry can raise α; an UPPER entry can
lower β. If the tightened window closes, its bounds justify
a cutoff. Otherwise, continue searching.
Even an entry whose value cannot be reused can supply
a move-ordering hint.

Compatibility includes the horizon and evaluation rules.
A depth-eight heuristic minimax value need not equal the
depth-three value at the same state. To preserve an exact
fixed-horizon specification, reuse values for a matching
horizon and compatible semantics, or use a genuinely solved
game value whose meaning is horizon-independent.

Practical engines sometimes deliberately reuse deeper
results for shallower requests. That may be useful, but it
changes the exact fixed-horizon function being computed.
Do not justify it merely by saying “deeper is more accurate.”
Selective extensions, repetition rules, evaluation changes,
and root-relative mate-distance scores need compatible
treatment too.

Retain the call's original α and β when classifying
a completed result. A fail-low result at or below original
α is an upper bound; a fail-high result at or above
original β is a lower bound. A result strictly inside
the original window is exact when the search and all
reused bounds are compatible.
The current, repeatedly modified window alone is not
a sufficient record of the query.

## Chance nodes

A random event is not a MIN move. At a chance node with
outcome probabilities p_i and continuation values v_i,
use the expectation Σ p_i v_i, with probabilities summing
to one. MAX and MIN still optimize at their own decision
nodes. This extension is often called expectiminimax.

For a fair two-outcome event with values 2 and 8,
the expectation is 5, rather than the minimum 2 or
maximum 8. The probability model and utility scale determine
what that average means.

Ordinary alpha-beta cutoffs do not transfer unchanged:
a partially accumulated expectation can increase or decrease
when unseen outcomes are included. Safe pruning needs bounds
on their values and probabilities or another justified rule.

Hidden cards introduce a further issue: future choices
depend on what each player knows. Treating private
information as a fully observed chance outcome can give
a player information it should not possess.
That topic lies beyond this perfect-information introduction.

The next chapter explores sampling as another way to
allocate game-search effort. The fixed utility convention,
state identity, and distinction between estimates and
proofs remain important there.

## Further reading

- Shannon, [“Programming a Computer for Playing
  Chess”](https://doi.org/10.1080/14786445008521796) (1950).
  A foundational account of the partnership between search
  and static evaluation.
- Knuth and Moore,
  [“An Analysis of Alpha-Beta Pruning”](https://doi.org/10.1016/0004-3702(75)90019-3)
  (1975). Explains alpha-beta's behavior and why move
  ordering can change its cost so substantially.

# Week 10: Beyond the Basics

The preceding methods provide a vocabulary for new search
designs: priorities, lower bounds, incumbents, duplicate
dominance, constraints, adversarial values, and measured
resource costs. This chapter uses that vocabulary to study
bounded suboptimal search, anytime certificates, bidirectional
search, Monte Carlo tree search, and multi-agent pathfinding.

These are extensions with different purposes. Some trade
solution quality for a different exploration order.
Others use two search directions, sampled outcomes, or
structured successor generation. Understanding which
information justifies a guarantee remains more useful than
memorizing another algorithm name.

## Weighted A*

A* selects minimum g+h. **Weighted A*** instead selects

**g+w·h, where w≥1.**

Keep g as actual path cost and h as a nonnegative admissible
remaining-cost estimate, zero at goals. Use strict best-g
improvements, skip stale queue entries, and reopen improved
states. Accept a goal only on a nonstale minimum removal.

For finite graphs with nonnegative costs, this version
returns a solution costing at most w times the optimum.
For potentially infinite graphs, finite branching and costs
bounded below by a positive ε provide a useful sufficient
condition for finite progress to a finite-cost goal.

Let C* be optimal cost. Until an optimal route is completed,
correct duplicate handling preserves a frontier prefix n
of that route with no worse than its optimal prefix cost.
Admissibility gives g(n)+h(n)≤C*. Since g(n)≥0 and w≥1,

**g(n)+w·h(n) ≤ w·(g(n)+h(n)) ≤ w·C*.**

When a goal of cost C is selected, its weighted key is C.
It cannot exceed that eligible prefix's key.
Therefore C≤w·C*.

The proof depends on retaining useful improved arrivals.
A permanent closed set is not automatically justified by
the consistency of the original h: multiplying h by w
can destroy consistency for the original edge costs.
Use the stated reopening implementation unless another
argument establishes the needed bound.

Consider two frontier entries with (g,h) values (2,8) and
(8,3). Ordinary A* assigns 10 and 11, preferring the first.
At w=2, the keys are 18 and 14, preferring the second.
Weight changes ordering; it does not change the actual
cost of either path.

This may find an acceptable goal sooner, but faster runtime
is not guaranteed on every instance. A larger weight also
weakens the worst-case solution-quality bound.
Report the weight, returned cost, and measured effort.
An inadmissible h does not inherit this w-factor proof.

## Anytime search and certified gaps

An **anytime optimizer** retains a feasible incumbent of
cost U while continuing to search. For minimization, U
is an upper bound: C*≤U. A lower bound explains how much
improvement could remain.

Suppose the search preserves all unresolved possibilities
through a correctly maintained frontier F. Every entry
has an admissible completion bound g+h. Account for improved
states awaiting reopening, and evaluate certificates between
completed expansion steps so pending child generation is
not silently omitted.

A valid global bound is

**L=min(U, min over eligible frontier entries of g+h).**

Take the minimum over an empty frontier as infinity.
Including U is essential: after finding an optimal
incumbent, all remaining frontier estimates can exceed U.
Their minimum alone would not lower-bound C*.

The certificate is L≤C*≤U. If U=15 and L=12, the optimum
lies between 12 and 15. The incumbent is at most 3 above
optimal, and, since L>0, at most 15/12=1.25 times optimal.
If the frontier minimum later rises to 18, the certificate
uses min(15,18)=15 and proves the incumbent optimal.

If L=0, U/L does not provide a useful finite ratio.
The additive gap U−L still makes sense. With no incumbent,
there is no feasible upper-bound answer to return.

Weighted keys g+w·h are not admissible lower bounds when
w>1. Choose work by that key if desired, but compute a
certificate from g+h or another justified bound.
A weighted queue's front need not minimize unweighted g+h;
maintaining both minima may require another queue or a scan.

An incumbent permits pruning a branch whose valid lower
bound is at least U when only one optimal answer is needed.
At frontier exhaustion, a retained incumbent is optimal
if all discarded branches were soundly handled.
If the search is restarted, certificates must be derived
from the new search's actual coverage, not an old queue
that has been discarded.

An early aggressive search can supply U to a separate
proof-oriented search. Alternatively, one algorithm can
improve the incumbent and bound together.
The interface is a feasible answer and a justified gap,
not merely a stream of increasingly plausible candidates.

## Bidirectional shortest-path search

For a known start s and goal t, search forward from s and
backward from t. In a directed graph, backward expansion
uses reversed edges with the original edge costs.
Each direction can use Dijkstra's nonnegative-cost rule.

A joined route supplies an upper bound μ. A shared
discovered vertex v gives an actual route costing
g_forward(v)+g_backward(v). Joining across an original edge
u→v can similarly combine a forward prefix, that edge,
and a backward suffix.

The first discovered meeting need not be optimal.
Consider s→a costing 1 and a→t costing 100, versus
s→b costing 50 and b→t costing 50.
After forward expansion of s, both prefixes are known.
If backward expansion of t considers predecessor a first,
the first joined candidate costs 101.
Considering b establishes a better candidate of 100.
Stopping at the first meeting even interrupts a necessary
comparison within this tiny example.

A standard bidirectional Dijkstra discipline is:

1. Maintain correct distance labels and queues in each
   direction, removing stale minima.
2. Expand a minimum-distance entry in the selected direction
   and perform the usual nonnegative-cost relaxations.
3. Update μ whenever discovered information joins the two
   directions into an actual complete route, including
   relevant crossing edges.
4. Stop when the valid queue minima satisfy m_f+m_b≥μ.

The stopping proof needs the joining discipline, not just
the formula. If a potentially cheaper path already crosses
the settled regions, its relevant join must have been
considered in μ. Otherwise it has an unresolved gap whose
forward prefix and backward suffix cost at least m_f and
m_b. Such a route cannot improve μ once their sum reaches μ.

An empty queue also needs explicit handling.
If one direction has exhausted its reachable region and
no join exists, there is no s-to-t path. If a joined route
exists, the algorithm's exhaustion and join invariant
settle its cost without pretending infinity is an ordinary
queue entry.

Two directions can reduce work greatly in roughly symmetric
spaces, but reverse successor generation may be hard.
The goal might describe many acceptable states rather than
one known endpoint. Two frontiers also consume memory,
and heuristic bidirectional search needs more careful
bounds than substituting two A* queues into this rule.

## Monte Carlo tree search

Minimax evaluates an adversarial tree using terminal values
or a horizon evaluator. **Monte Carlo tree search**, MCTS,
instead allocates repeated samples among actions.
A typical iteration has four stages:

1. Select a path through currently stored tree nodes.
2. Expand an untried action when appropriate.
3. Estimate its continuation through a rollout or value model.
4. Back up the result and update visit counts.

A rollout can play legal moves to a terminal state using a
simple policy. Its result might be +1 for a MAX win, 0 for
a draw, and −1 for a loss. Keep the fixed MAX perspective
from [Week 9](09-adversarial.md).

Let Q_i be the mean sampled MAX reward for child i, N_i its
visit count, and N the parent's count. A common exploration
bonus has the form

**B_i=c·sqrt(ln(N)/N_i), with c>0.**

Try unvisited actions before using this expression.
The division is undefined at N_i=0.
The parameter c has meaning relative to reward scale.

For a MAX node, select a child maximizing Q_i+B_i.
For a MIN node, select one maximizing −Q_i+B_i.
Equivalently, MIN minimizes Q_i−B_i.
The exploration bonus must encourage poorly sampled actions
at either player's node. Simply minimizing Q_i+B_i at MIN
would instead penalize a large uncertainty bonus.

Under this convention, backup adds the same MAX-perspective
reward to every visited node's accumulated reward and
increments each visit count. Do not also negate the reward
on alternate levels. Other perspective conventions work,
but their selection and backup rules must match.

For example, let N=16 and c=0.5. A child with N_i=4 has
bonus about 0.416; one with N_i=1 has bonus about 0.833.
At a MAX node, means 0.5 and 0.25 give selection scores
about 0.916 and 1.083. The less-tested action receives
another sample despite its lower observed mean.

This exploration rule is often called UCT.
Its confidence-inspired expression does not turn every
finite search into a calibrated statistical guarantee.
Tree policies change as search learns, descendants can
be sampled unevenly, and rollout outcomes can be biased
relative to optimal play.

At the final decision, the exploration bonus is generally
not the value to maximize. A common choice is the most
visited root action; another is a suitably supported mean.
Specify the recommendation rule separately from the rule
used to allocate samples.

MCTS can miss rare decisive replies under a small budget.
Random rollouts may almost never execute an important tactic.
A learned value model can replace or shorten rollouts,
but its errors become part of the search behavior.
Report budget, policy, perspective, reward scale, and
empirical reliability rather than treating a sampled mean
as a minimax certificate.

## Many agents sharing one graph

**Multi-agent pathfinding**, MAPF, seeks compatible paths for
several agents. Individually shortest routes can collide
at a shared vertex or a narrow passage.
A joint state records one location per agent, making the
configuration space grow rapidly with team size.

A common discrete-time model allows each agent to move
to a neighbor or wait. Collision rules are part of the
instance definition. Two agents may be forbidden from
occupying one vertex simultaneously and from swapping
the endpoints of an edge in one step. Arrival behavior
also matters: does an agent remain at its goal?

The objective must be specified too.
**Makespan** measures when the last agent finishes.
**Sum of costs** adds agents' path costs under the stated
waiting and arrival convention. A plan that improves one
objective can worsen the other.

Conflict-Based Search illustrates a structured alternative
to blindly enumerating every joint action. It proposes
individual paths, finds a conflict, and branches on
constraints excluding one participant or the other from
that conflict. Individual replanning supplies paths
respecting the accumulated constraints.
The conflict tree can still be large; decomposition does
not remove combinatorial difficulty.

Keisuke Okumura's LaCAM work offers a more recent connection
between configuration search and constraint-driven successor
generation. Its 2023 AAAI paper presents a complete method
using lazy constraint addition to organize the generation
of joint configurations. The useful design idea is to avoid
materializing all joint moves eagerly.

The 2023 IJCAI follow-up, LaCAM*, develops an anytime
extension with eventual optimality under its stated
accumulated-transition-cost model. Eventual optimality
does not supply a deadline by which the optimum must appear.
The distinction between an early feasible plan and a
completed optimality argument remains essential.

These papers are examples of current research directions,
not a claim that one planner wins on every MAPF instance.
Their model, objective, completeness conditions, benchmark
distribution, and resource budget determine how to interpret
reported results.

## Guidance and proof in new methods

Learned models can suggest promising successors, conflicts,
or moves. If guidance only changes ordering inside an
otherwise complete search, completeness can survive when
all required alternatives are eventually considered.
Permanent learned pruning or replacing an admissible bound
with an unchecked prediction needs a new argument.

The same questions apply without machine learning.
Does a new data structure preserve duplicate identity?
Does a parallel termination rule account for in-flight work?
Does a faster priority supply a valid bound, or only a
preference? Does an exact inner solver make the outer
method complete, or only solve one neighborhood?

The methods in this chapter can be combined, but their
guarantees do not combine automatically.
A weighted search can supply an incumbent to a certifying
search. An anytime MAPF method can use ordering guidance.
A game search can use sampled evaluations.
State the model, retained information, and stopping rule
before inheriting any promise from a familiar name.

## Further reading

- Hansen and Zhou,
  [“Anytime Heuristic Search”](https://doi.org/10.1613/jair.2096)
  (2007). Develops heuristic search that improves answers
  while maintaining information about solution quality.
- Kocsis and Szepesvári,
  [“Bandit Based Monte-Carlo Planning”](https://doi.org/10.1007/11871842_29)
  (2006). Introduces UCT and its combination of sampling
  with exploration-guided tree search.
- Okumura, [“LaCAM: Search-Based Algorithm for Quick
  Multi-Agent Pathfinding”](https://ojs.aaai.org/index.php/AAAI/article/view/26377)
  (2023). A concrete example of constraints organizing
  successor generation in a large joint space.
- Okumura, [“Improving LaCAM for Scalable Eventually
  Optimal Multi-Agent Pathfinding”](https://www.ijcai.org/proceedings/2023/28)
  (2023). Connects early feasibility, continued search,
  and eventual optimality in the same application family.

# Recovery review and pending integration

2026-10-22 Pacific. This note concerns the recovered first draft.

## State on disk

Root read back complete chapters 01,02,06,07 and partial 08.
Root completed 08 and added schedule.svg before disconnection.
Algorithm checks, worked-example checks and extension checks passed.
Six then-existing SVGs were visually inspected in Chromium.
Figures in completed chapters link to full-size SVG originals.

## New reviewed text

Recovered chapters 03,04,05,09,10 are original explanations,
approximately 2,100–2,400 words each by the source-check counter.
They contain no exercises, implementation-language listings,
unconfigured LaTeX or unresolved placeholders.
They use the accepted chapter sequence and existing notation.

Root corrected these draft problems before checkpointing:
- Systematic search can use heuristic ordering; coverage is the
  relevant distinction.
- Goal-on-removal BFS can generate the next layer; distinguish its
  O(b^(d+1)) bound from goal-on-generation O(b^d).
- The DFS example route has three edges; the BFS route has two.
- IDDFS's constant-factor regular-tree comparison assumes b>1;
  a chain gives quadratic regeneration.
- Removed an unverified/misattributed Korf thesis reference.
- Replaced mutable predecessor ambiguity with immutable path
  entries in the best-first pseudocode.
- Corrected chapter-order transitions and removed raw LaTeX and
  redundant ASCII puzzle boards.
- Memory depth D means maximum depth actually reached; it need
  not be the shallowest solution depth.
- Initialized the IDA* path and copied a successful path before
  restoration; retained RBFS infinity-exhaustion handling.
- Made MAX a fixed player throughout game search; qualified
  transposition-table horizon compatibility and fingerprint risk.
- Corrected weighted-A* arithmetic: (g,h)=(2,8),(8,3) gives
  ordinary keys10,11 and weight-two keys18,14.
- Anytime lower bound is min(U,min eligible frontier(g+h)),
  including the incumbent and pending/reopened work.
- At MIN, fixed-MAX UCT explores by maximizing -Q+bonus,
  not by minimizing Q+bonus.
- Made the bidirectional joining and stopping assumptions explicit.

An independent agent checked supplied excerpts for AC-3,
coloring deltas, partition neighbors, annealing/restart math,
finite-domain backtracking, the courier relaxation, and the
schedule. It found no substantive error. Its wording caveats
(singleton AC-3 domains; absolute-imbalance E) were already
explicit. It did not review the full chapters or SAT encoding.
SAT equivalence and the AC-3 trace were separately enumerated
by root in check_examples.py.

## Primary reference checks

Metadata/relevance checked through publisher or author pages:
- Dijkstra1959, DOI10.1007/BF01386390.
- Korf1985 iterative deepening, author bibliography and cited DOI
  10.1016/0004-3702(85)90084-0.
- Dechter/Pearl1985, DOI10.1145/3828.3830.
- Korf/Felner2002, DOI10.1016/S0004-3702(01)00092-3.
- Korf1993 RBFS, DOI10.1016/0004-3702(93)90045-D.
- Shannon1950, DOI10.1080/14786445008521796.
- Knuth/Moore1975, DOI10.1016/0004-3702(75)90019-3.
- Hansen/Zhou2007, DOI10.1613/jair.2096; author-hosted arXiv
  record1110.2737 confirms journal year despite2011 posting.
- Kocsis/Szepesvari2006, DOI10.1007/11871842_29, Springer.
- Okumura LaCAM2023, AAAI proceedings26377.
- Okumura LaCAM*2023, IJCAI proceedings2023/28. Publisher
  abstract explicitly conditions eventual optimality on
  accumulated transition costs.

Hart/Nilsson/Raphael1968 DOI10.1109/TSSC.1968.300136 is a
bibliographic citation. IEEE automated access reached a
robot-verification page; retain this access limitation rather
than claiming a full primary-paper review.
No cited paper was comprehensively audited in this campaign.
The new chapter arguments and examples were written independently;
no source prose, tables, pseudocode listings, or figures adapted.
No actual Wikipedia adaptation requires a revision attribution.

## Pending after reconnect

Read exact JSON archive on the recovery Page and write files at
their paths relative to /home/bart/work/search/book.
Its src/figures/alpha-beta.svg is an original new figure.
Do not overwrite saved chapters1,2,6,7,8 with stale copies.

Run mdbook build and checks/check_book.py.
Run checks/check_browser.cjs and visually inspect new figure
and representative pages, including narrow and large-text views.
Extend worked-example checks for new traces if needed.
Update STATUS, README and source/review logs from actual results.
No completed full-book build or browser check is claimed yet.
Do not commit or push.

notes: All files above await local integration. Chapters 01,02,06,07,08 and existing assets/checks are already saved there. Read research/recovery-review.md for results and remaining checks. Original contributions CC BY-SA 4.0.
